title: Modern Chemical Manufactures — Ammonia, Nitric Acid, Sulphuric Acid, NaOH, Soda Ash and Urea
topicTitle: Modern Chemical Manufactures: manufacture of ammonia, nitric acid, sulphuric acid, sodium hydroxide, sodium carbonate and urea
notes: **Importance of chemical manufactures:** Modern society depends on large-scale chemical production for fertilisers, cleaning agents, building materials, pharmaceuticals, and plastics. The chemicals covered here are among the most produced worldwide by mass.

**Ammonia — Haber's Process:** $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$, $\Delta H = -92.4$ kJ/mol (exothermic). **Conditions:** (1) Pressure: 150–300 atm (high pressure favours NH₃ by Le Chatelier — 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas). (2) Temperature: 400–500°C (compromise — low T favours yield but rate is too slow). (3) Catalyst: finely divided iron with $K_2O$ and $Al_2O_3$ promoters. **Yield:** ~15% per pass; unreacted $N_2$ and $H_2$ are recycled. **Uses:** fertilisers (ammonium nitrate, urea), explosives, refrigerant, nitric acid production.

**Hydrogen production for Haber's process:** Hydrogen is obtained from natural gas (methane) via steam reforming: $CH_4 + H_2O \rightarrow CO + 3H_2$ (800–900°C, Ni catalyst), followed by the water-gas shift: $CO + H_2O \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2$. Nitrogen is obtained by liquefaction and fractional distillation of air.

**Nitric acid — Ostwald's Process:** (Step 1) Oxidation of ammonia: $4NH_3(g) + 5O_2(g) \rightarrow 4NO(g) + 6H_2O(g)$, $\Delta H = -904$ kJ/mol. Catalyst: Pt-Rh alloy gauze at 900°C. (Step 2) Oxidation of NO: $2NO(g) + O_2(g) \rightarrow 2NO_2(g)$. (Step 3) Absorption in water: $3NO_2(g) + H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2HNO_3(aq) + NO(g)$. The NO is recycled. **Concentration:** ~68% HNO₃ by mass (azeotropic mixture). **Uses:** fertilisers (ammonium nitrate), explosives (TNT, nitroglycerin), etching metals.

**Sulphuric acid — Contact Process:** (Step 1) Sulphur burning: $S(s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow SO_2(g)$. (Step 2) Catalytic oxidation: $2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3(g)$, $\Delta H = -196$ kJ/mol. Conditions: 450°C, 1–2 atm, $V_2O_5$ catalyst. (Step 3) Absorption: $SO_3$ is NOT absorbed directly in water (forms corrosive mist). Instead, absorbed in conc. $H_2SO_4$: $SO_3 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow H_2S_2O_7$ (oleum). (Step 4) Dilution: $H_2S_2O_7 + H_2O \rightarrow 2H_2SO_4$. **Uses:** fertilisers (superphosphate), battery acid, petroleum refining, detergent production. It is the most produced chemical in the world (~200 million tonnes/year).

**Sodium hydroxide — Chlor-Alkali Process (Diaphragm Cell):** Electrolysis of brine (concentrated NaCl solution): $2NaCl(aq) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g) + Cl_2(g)$. **Anode (graphite):** $2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-$. **Cathode (steel):** $2H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2 + 2OH^-$. A diaphragm prevents $Cl_2$ and NaOH mixing. **Mercury cell** (being phased out): Na amalgam forms at Hg cathode, then reacts with water: $2Na(Hg) + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2$. **Uses:** soap/detergent manufacture, paper pulping, aluminium production, drain cleaners.

**Sodium carbonate — Solvay (Ammonia-Soda) Process:** (1) Brine is saturated with $NH_3$: $NaCl + H_2O + NH_3 \rightarrow$ ammoniated brine. (2) $CO_2$ is passed through: $NH_3 + CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow NH_4HCO_3$. (3) Sodium bicarbonate precipitates: $NH_4HCO_3 + NaCl \rightarrow NaHCO_3(s) + NH_4Cl$. (4) Heating: $2NaHCO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} Na_2CO_3 + CO_2 + H_2O$. The $CO_2$ is recycled. $NH_3$ is recovered from $NH_4Cl$ using $Ca(OH)_2$. **Uses:** glass manufacturing (70% of production), detergents, water softening, paper, textiles.

**Urea — Bosch-Meiser Process:** (1) Ammonium carbamate formation: $2NH_3(g) + CO_2(g) \xrightarrow{180°C, 150 atm} NH_2COONH_4(l)$. (2) Decomposition to urea: $NH_2COONH_4(l) \xrightarrow{\Delta} NH_2CONH_2(l) + H_2O(g)$. The reaction is carried out at 180–200°C and 140–175 atm. Water is removed by evaporation; excess $NH_3$ and $CO_2$ are recycled. **Uses:** nitrogen fertiliser (46% N by mass), animal feed, formaldehyde resins, automotive diesel exhaust treatment (AdBlue). It is the world's most widely used nitrogen fertiliser.

**Le Chatelier's principle in industrial processes:** All the above processes use Le Chatelier's principle to optimise yield: (1) Haber's — high P, moderate T. (2) Contact — moderate T, excess $O_2$, removal of $SO_3$. (3) Solvay — precipitation drives the reaction forward. (4) Urea — high P favours the forward reaction (gas → liquid).

**Environmental considerations:** (1) Haber's process consumes ~1–2% of world's energy supply (mainly for $H_2$ production). (2) Contact process $SO_2$ emissions cause acid rain. (3) Chlor-alkali mercury cells cause mercury pollution — being replaced by membrane cells. (4) Fertiliser runoff causes eutrophication in water bodies.

**Relative global production (approximate):** (1) Sulphuric acid: ~260 million tonnes/year. (2) Ammonia: ~180 million tonnes/year. (3) Sodium hydroxide: ~90 million tonnes/year. (4) Sodium carbonate: ~70 million tonnes/year. (5) Nitric acid: ~60 million tonnes/year. (6) Urea: ~180 million tonnes/year.

**Key reaction conditions summary:**
- Haber (NH₃): 200 atm, 450°C, Fe catalyst
- Ostwald (HNO₃): Pt-Rh, 900°C
- Contact (H₂SO₄): 1–2 atm, 450°C, V₂O₅
- Chlor-alkali (NaOH): aqueous electrolysis, diaphragm/membrane cell
- Solvay (Na₂CO₃): room temp, CO₂ absorption
- Urea: 180°C, 150 atm
confusion: **Why $SO_3$ is not absorbed directly in water (Contact process):** Direct absorption of $SO_3$ in water produces a fine corrosive mist of $H_2SO_4$ that is difficult to condense. Instead, $SO_3$ is absorbed in concentrated $H_2SO_4$ to form oleum ($H_2S_2O_7$), which is then safely diluted with measured water.

**Why moderate temperature in Haber's process:** The reaction is exothermic, so low temperature favours yield (Le Chatelier). However, too low a temperature makes the rate impractically slow. 450°C is a compromise that gives reasonable yield (~15% per pass) with acceptable rate, enabled by the iron catalyst.

**Difference between Solvay and Contact processes:** Solvay produces sodium carbonate (a salt) from brine and limestone. Contact produces sulphuric acid from sulphur. They share the name 'process' but are completely different in chemistry and purpose. Do not confuse the reagents and products.

**Mercury cell vs. diaphragm cell vs. membrane cell in chlor-alkali:** Mercury cell gives purest NaOH but causes mercury pollution. Diaphragm cell is cheaper but NaOH contains NaCl impurity. Membrane cell (modern) combines purity with environmental safety — it uses an ion-exchange membrane instead of a diaphragm or mercury.

**Urea vs. ammonium nitrate as fertiliser:** Both supply nitrogen, but urea (46% N) has higher nitrogen content than ammonium nitrate (35% N). Urea is also less hygroscopic and safer to transport (ammonium nitrate can be explosive under certain conditions, as seen in the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing and 2020 Beirut explosion).
practice: In the Haber process, explain why a pressure of 200 atm is used despite the high cost of maintaining such pressure. **Solution:** The reaction $N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3$ involves 4 moles of gas producing 2 moles. High pressure shifts equilibrium to the right (Le Chatelier), increasing yield. At 200 atm, yield is ~35% vs. ~0.1% at 1 atm. The cost of compression is offset by the value of the product and recycling of unreacted gases.

Write the balanced equations for the Ostwald process and identify the catalyst used in each step. **Solution:** Step 1: $4NH_3 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 4NO + 6H_2O$ (Pt-Rh catalyst, 900°C). Step 2: $2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2$ (no catalyst, occurs spontaneously on cooling). Step 3: $3NO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow 2HNO_3 + NO$ (absorption tower, NO recycled).

In the Solvay process, explain the role of $NH_3$ and why it is recycled. **Solution:** $NH_3$ makes the brine alkaline, allowing it to absorb $CO_2$ more effectively to form $NH_4HCO_3$. It is recovered from $NH_4Cl$ by treatment with $Ca(OH)_2$: $2NH_4Cl + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCl_2 + 2H_2O + 2NH_3$. Recycling makes the process economically viable.

Calculate the mass of $Fe_2O_3$ required to produce 1000 kg of Fe in a blast furnace. (Atomic masses: Fe = 56, O = 16) **Solution:** $Fe_2O_3 \rightarrow 2Fe + \dfrac{3}{2}O_2$. Molar mass $Fe_2O_3$ = 160 g/mol; 2Fe = 112 g. Mass ratio: $160/112 = 1.429$. Mass of $Fe_2O_3$ = $1000 \times 1.429 = 1429$ kg.

Why is the membrane cell preferred over the mercury cell in modern chlor-alkali industry? **Solution:** Mercury cells produce NaOH free of NaCl but release toxic mercury into the environment, causing pollution and health hazards (Minamata disease). Membrane cells use a selective cation-exchange membrane that allows $Na^+$ through but blocks $Cl^-$ and $OH^-$, producing pure NaOH without mercury. This makes membrane cells both environmentally safe and economically competitive.
universalFacts: Sulphuric acid is the single most produced chemical globally (~260 million tonnes/year) and is considered a key indicator of a nation's industrial strength.
The Haber process supplies approximately half of the nitrogen in the global food supply through fertilisers — an estimated 40–50% of the nitrogen in human bodies comes from Haber-derived fertilisers.

The Contact process was developed by Peregrine Phillips in 1831 (sulfuric acid from pyrite) and modernised with the $V_2O_5$ catalyst in 1878 by process engineer Michael Sumersheffi and later commercialised by the Badische Anilin- & Soda-Fabrik (BASF).
The Solvay process, invented by Ernest Solvay in 1861, replaced the expensive and polluting Leblanc process. It remains the dominant method for soda ash production worldwide.

Urea was the first organic compound synthesised from inorganic precursors (Wöhler, 1828: $NH_4CN \rightarrow NH_2CONH_2$), overthrowing the vitalism theory that organic compounds required a 'vital force'.
